query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating on a Cu matrix, whose overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation behavior across different temperatures remain unclear, what single intervention could improve its wear resistance under sliding conditions spanning different temperatures, friction velocities, and wear depths? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to the unchanged FeNiCrCoCu coating tested under identical conditions, defines the operating limits of the prediction, cites supporting evidence from the introduction, and proposes a falsification experiment capable of resolving microscopic deformation during wear.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of Tungsten (W) to the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating will improve its wear resistance under sliding conditions spanning different temperatures, friction velocities, and wear depths.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating on a Cu matrix
generation.intervention: Addition of Tungsten (W) to the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating
generation.conditions: Sliding conditions with varying temperatures, friction velocities, and wear depths
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) consisting of various nanocrystalline (NC) oxides on the worn surface
generation.mechanism: The incorporation of W improves the wear resistance of the cladding coating by reducing the friction coefficient and promoting the formation of a protective oxide layer, which assists in enhancing the friction interface while providing solid lubrication
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating with the addition of W, resulting in a lower friction coefficient and specific wear rate compared to the unchanged FeNiCrCoCu coating tested under identical conditions
generation.baseline: Unchanged FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating on a Cu matrix
generation.boundary: Temperature range: room temperature to 800 °C, friction velocities: 5 mm/s to 500 mm/s, wear depths: 0.001 g to 0.01 g
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of the improved wear resistance with the addition of W is not fully understood and requires further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Sliding wear test with varying temperatures, friction velocities, and wear depths
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of W does not result in a significant reduction in friction coefficient and specific wear rate, and the worn surface morphology does not show evidence of a protective oxide layer, then the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Thus, if cooperative heterostructures capable of releasing frictional stress in stages are configured in the alloy, it is expected to suppress the sliding-induced deformation. In contrast, upon wear at high temperatures (≥600 °C), the wear behavior of the material becomes quite complex, stemming from the prevalence of surface adhesion and tribo-oxidation at the friction interface [,]. High-temperature sliding tends to soften the metallic surface that endows the near-surface material susceptible to chemical instability caused by counterbody materials or environmental oxygen, triggering severe delamination wear and composition segregation at the friction interface that exacerbates wear [,]. Materials become more dependent on tribochemical protection upon high-temperature wear due to deterioration in stiffness [,]. Tribo-oxidation may promote the formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) consisting of various nanocrystalline (NC) oxides on the worn surface, which assists in enhancing the friction interface while providing solid lubrication [,,]. Figure 8 illustrates the FeCoCrNiAlWx high-entropy alloy cladding coating with friction coefficient curves, as the W content increases from x = 0 to x = 0.8. The friction coefficients of the cladding coatings with different W compositions display significant fluctuations during the running-in stage of the friction experiment, gradually stabilizing over time. During the stable phase, as the W content rises from x = 0 to x = 0.8, the average friction coefficients of the cladding coatings are 0.669, 0.664, 0.617, 0.544, and 0.527, respectively. Overall, the friction coefficient decreases with increasing W content, indicating that the incorporation of W improves the wear resistance of the cladding coating. It is noteworthy that the friction coefficients for x = 0 are similar with x = 0.2, suggesting minimal enhancement of wear resistance with low W content. However, the friction coefficients for x = 0.6 are close with x = 0.8; this suggests that a further increase in W content results in a saturation effect on enhancing wear resistance.
